chapter_en: The Sanctity of the Names and Their Burial

sections.title_en: 1. The Names and the Sacred Writings
sections.body_en:
All sanctified things are sacred writings that contain holy Names. True, when the Temple stood there was holiness also in the Temple and its consecrated objects, which contain no Names; but since the Temple was destroyed, all sanctified things are the sacred writings, such as Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot, which contain holy Names. Objects intended to protect them or add beauty to them also have holiness, and once they are worn out they must be put in geniza; they are called 'accessories of holiness' (tashmishei kedusha). However, there is no holiness in objects through which mitzvot are fulfilled that contain no writing, such as tzitzit, a shofar and a sukka, and they are called 'accessories of mitzva' (tashmishei mitzva) (below 14:8).

In order to understand the meaning of the holiness in sacred writings, we must first explain that no created being is able to know the Holy One, blessed be He, in His glory and essence. All that we are able to know is His revelation in the world, as He was revealed to the people of Israel and to His prophets, headed by Moshe our teacher. The essence of the Divine revelation finds expression in the holy Names of the Holy One, blessed be He, through which God chose to reveal Himself to the world, each Name expressing a particular revelation of God; and above all the Names is the Explicit Name (Ha-Shem Ha-Meforash), which expresses the whole of the Divine revelation (as explained in the next halakha).

The whole Torah, too, is considered the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, because the Torah, with all its guidance and mitzvot, is the unfolding in detail of the Divine revelation to the world. As the Ramban wrote (in his introduction to the book of Bereshit): "We further possess a true tradition that the whole Torah is the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He". And so they said in the Zohar (part 2, 124a, in translation): "The whole Torah is the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and one who engages in it is as if he engages in the holy Name, because the whole Torah is one holy Name, a supernal Name, a Name that includes all the Names, and one who subtracts one letter from it – it is as if he blemished the holy Name". They further said (there 90b): "One who merits the Torah – merits His holy Name". And so the Sages learned (Berakhot 21a) that it is a mitzva to recite a blessing before Torah study from what is said (Devarim 32:3): "For I will proclaim the name of the Lord; ascribe greatness to our God". That is, in preparation for proclaiming the Name of God, which is Torah study, one must express the greatness of God by means of a blessing. And so the Sages said (Avot 3:6) that when Israel engage in Torah the Shekhina dwells among them, and even one person who studies Torah alone merits a certain measure of the indwelling of the Shekhina, as it is said (Shemot 20:20): "In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned I will come to you and bless you". Thus Torah study is considered a mention of the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, for the purpose of the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He, as also the purpose of the whole Torah, is to reveal the word of God and His blessing to the world. Therefore there is holiness also in sacred writings that contain no holy Names, although their holiness is not on the level of the holiness of writings that contain holy Names (below halakha 15, note 18).

The holy Names are the concentrated expression of the Divine spirit of life through which God gives life to all created beings, and the Torah is the full expression of the Divine spirit of life that gives life to the world. As the Sages said: "When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world – He looked into it, into the Torah, and created the world" (Zohar part 2, 161a; and so in Bereshit Rabba 1:1). Therefore the existence of the world depended on Israel's accepting the Torah (Shabbat 88a), and its continued existence depends on Israel's engaging in Torah study (Pesaḥim 68b; Nefesh Ha-Ḥayim 4:11).

The Name of God, which is also called 'the Explicit Name', is 'Y-H-V-H', which alludes to God having been, being and going to be, and always bringing the world into being (Tur, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5:1; Tanya, Sha'ar Ha-Yiḥud Ve-ha-Emuna 4). And concerning this God said to Moshe (Shemot 6:3): "And I appeared to Avraham, to Yitzḥak and to Ya'akov as El Shaddai, but by My name Y-H-V-H I did not make Myself known to them". And from the time that God began to bring Israel out of Egypt, He became known to Israel by His Explicit Name, as it is said (there 7:17): "Thus says Y-H-V-H: By this you shall know that I am Y-H-V-H – behold, I will strike with the rod that is in my hand upon the waters that are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood".

Because of the great holiness of the Explicit Name, only in the Temple did the kohanim say it, in the Priestly Blessing (Sota 38a). And after the death of Shimon Ha-Tzaddik, who was High Priest at the beginning of the days of the Second Temple, they no longer merited the revelation of the Shekhina, and since that was so, the kohanim stopped pronouncing the Explicit Name. In addition, they were afraid to say it lest an unworthy person learn it (Yoma 39b; Kiddushin 71a, and Rashi there; Rambam, Laws of Prayer 14:10). Similarly, the High Priest would pronounce the Explicit Name ten times in the Yom Kippur service. In the early generations he would raise his voice, and when Israel declined from their level and there were unworthy people among them – he would say it in a low voice, so that even those standing near him would not hear the Explicit Name (Rambam, Laws of the Yom Kippur Service 2:6; see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 20:1-2).

As stated, outside the Temple one does not say the Explicit Name as it is written; rather, wherever the Explicit Name (Y-H-V-H) is mentioned in the Torah or in the siddur, one reads it as the Name of Lordship (Ado-nai), which is second to it in importance (Pesaḥim 50a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5:1). And when it is adjacent to the Name of Lordship, it is read 'Elohim', and then it is also vocalised with the vowels of the Name Elohim (for example Bereshit 15:2: "And Avram said: Ado-nai Y-H-V-H, what will You give me", and likewise in Yeḥezkel 33:11: "Say to them: As I live, says Ado-nai Y-H-V-H, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked").

Because of the great holiness of the Explicit Name, people try to minimise even its writing, and therefore I have written its letters separated, so that holiness will not take effect on it. Some say that it is forbidden even to mention its letters one after the other, and therefore people are accustomed to say: "Yod Ki Vav Ki", 'Ki' instead of 'Hei' (Radbaz part 5, 1408, following Tosafot; Ḥayei Adam 5:27).1

notes_en.en:
Pesaḥim (50a): "It is written (Shemot 3:15): This is My name for ever (le-olam), and this is My remembrance for all generations. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Not as I am written am I read; I am written with yod-heh (Y-H-V-H), and I am read with alef-dalet (A-D-N-Y)". Rashi explained that 'le-olam' is written without a 'vav', in the sense of concealment (he'elem), for one must conceal the Name and not pronounce it. According to Abba Shaul, one who pronounces the Name by its letters – has no share in the World to Come (Mishna Sanhedrin 10:1). And the Tanna Kamma too, who disagreed with Abba Shaul, agrees that it is forbidden (Yad Rama, Sanhedrin 90a; Me'iri). The Rambam holds like the Tanna Kamma, for he did not count him among those who have no share in the World to Come (Einayim La-Mishpat, Sanhedrin 90a). However, the Semag (positive commandments 4) wrote simply that he has no share in the World to Come (and so wrote Ḥayei Adam 5:27), and the Semag explained that "one who pronounces the Name by its letters" transgresses the positive mitzva to fear God. It is further explained in Avoda Zara (18a) that in order 'to train himself' it is permitted to pronounce the Name by its letters in private, and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon was punished because he did so in public.
In Responsa Radbaz (5:35) he learned from Tosafot (Avoda Zara 18a, s.v. 'Hoge') that one should not say the letters of the Explicit Name in sequence, and instead of 'Hei' one should say 'Ki'. And so wrote Ḥayei Adam (5:27) and Responsa Torah Lishma 491. In contrast, Rav Yissakhar Tamar explained that although people are accustomed to be stringent, all the Rishonim who explained this sugya wrote 'Hei' and not 'Ki', and since they did not qualify it, it stands to reason that that is also what they said. And this is the custom of the immigrants from Yemen (Alei Tamar, Sanhedrin 10:1).

sections.body_en:
Besides the Explicit Name of God, there are further Names by which God is called in the Tanakh, and each Name expresses a particular revelation of His in the world (Shemot Rabba 3:6). In general, these Names express His being the Creator of the world and its Master, and that He gives life to the world and sustains it, watches over His creatures, pays a good reward to the righteous, punishes the wicked and is faithful to His promise, and many further deep meanings with which the sages of faith and Kabbala engaged at length.

The second Name in importance is the Name of Lordship: 'Ado-nai', whose meaning is that God is the Master of all. The halakhic significance of its status is that when the Explicit Name (Y-H-V-H) is written in the Torah or in the siddur, one says the Name of Lordship in its place. Generally, when Scripture relates that people turn to God, they turn to Him by the Name of Lordship (Bereshit 18:27, 30-32; Shemot 5:22, and elsewhere).

The further Names are: 'El', after the kindness that God bestows upon the world. 'Elohim', whose meaning is that He is mighty without limit and the possessor of all powers. 'Shaddai', which expresses His ability to set limits to the life He bestows upon the world in a precise manner, and to give reward to the righteous and punishment to the wicked. 'Tzeva'ot', which expresses His being the ruler and leader of all the forces in the world, all of which are His hosts (tzeva'ot) that reveal His will. 'Ehyeh', which expresses His being revealed constantly in all times and in all dimensions.

Included in the Name 'Elohim' are also all the inflections of this Name, such as: 'Elohei', 'Eloheikhem', 'Eloheinu', and likewise 'Eloah'. Included in the Name Y-H-V-H is also the Name 'Yah', which expresses a supernal and hidden revelation that is grasped by ḥokhma and bina. All the Names of God must be treated with holiness: they may not be mentioned in vain, and it is likewise forbidden to erase them. However, the epithets with which God is praised, such as 'Gracious' (Ḥanun) and 'Merciful' (Raḥum), are not considered holy Names, and when necessary it is permitted to erase them.[2]

notes_en.en:
A baraita in Shevu'ot (35a): "These are the Names that may not be erased: such as El, Elohekha, Elohim, Eloheikhem, Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh, Alef-Dalet, and Yod-Hei, Shaddai, Tzeva'ot – these may not be erased. But Ha-Gadol, Ha-Gibbor, Ha-Nora, Ha-Addir, Ve-ha-Ḥazak, Ve-ha-Amitz, Ha-Izuz, Ḥanun Ve-Raḥum, Erekh Apayim, Ve-Rav Ḥesed – these may be erased". And in Avot de-Rabbi Natan (version A, 34): "The Holy One, blessed be He, is called by ten Names of praise, and these are they: the Name Alef-Dalet (Ado-nai), Yod-Hei-Vav-Hei (Y-H-V-H), Elohim, Eloah, Elohekha, Eloheikhem, El, Ehyeh, Shaddai, Tzeva'ot". The Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:2) wrote: "And they are seven Names: the Name written yod-hei-vav-hei, which is the Explicit Name; or the one written Ado-nai; and El; Eloah; and Elohim; and Elohei; and Shaddai; and Tzeva'ot". However, some read in his words 'Ehyeh' instead of 'El', and there are further readings (see Kesef Mishneh there). And although different counts of the Names that may not be erased are mentioned among the Rishonim, the difference concerns the manner of counting the Names, but it is agreed that the Names mentioned in the baraita have further inflections that were not mentioned (Responsa Rashbash 267; Responsa Radbaz 5:34; Baḥ, Yoreh De'ah 276:5). In halakha, all the Names of God are forbidden to be erased, including the Name 'Ehyeh', 'Yah', and all kinds of inflections of the Name 'Elohim' (see Shulḥan Arukh 276:9; Keset Ha-Sofer 11:5).
In Sha'arei Ora (fifth gate) he wrote: "Know and believe that the Name Y-H-V-H is the pillar to which all the sefirot – upper and lower – are attached, and in it they are united from below to above, and through it they receive their flow from above to below. And this is the Name that stands like the trunk of the tree, and all the other holy Names are like the branches of the tree, and all of them are united in it". And there he explains the Name 'Havaya' as corresponding to the ten sefirot: the tip of the 'yod' corresponds to keter, 'yod' – ḥokhma, 'heh' – bina, 'vav' – ḥesed, gevura, tiferet, netzaḥ, hod, yesod; 'heh' – malkhut. In addition, the sefirot correspond to the Names, as he wrote in Pardes Rimonim (gate 1, chapter 10, following Zohar Vayikra 10-11): "These sefirot are the ten Names that are not erased, and the Names and the sefirot – all is one thing, for the spirituality of the Names is the very sefirot": keter – Ehyeh, ḥokhma – Yah, bina – Y-H-V-H (vocalised as Elohim), ḥesed – El, gevura – Elohim, tiferet – Y-H-V-H (vocalised as Ado-nai), netzaḥ – Y-H-V-H Tzeva'ot, hod – Elohim Tzeva'ot, yesod – Shaddai (El Ḥai), malkhut – Ado-nai. And he explained this at length there in gate 20, chapters 1-13.

sections.title_en: 4. The Prohibition of Mentioning the Name of Heaven in Vain
sections.body_en:
It is a positive mitzva from the Torah to fear God, as it is said (Devarim 6:13; 10:20): "You shall fear the Lord your God". The main meaning of the mitzva is that we remember that God created the world and sustains it at every moment, and watches over and knows all that is done in it, and that we fear Him and fulfil His mitzvot. It is a kal va-ḥomer: if a person is afraid to defy the word of a king of flesh and blood, how much more so must he be afraid to defy the word of the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.

Also included in this mitzva is not to mention the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, needlessly. We have already learned (in halakha 3) that the Holy One, blessed be He, is called by several Names in the Torah, and each Name expresses a different aspect of the revelation of God in the world, and out of respect it is forbidden to mention one of these Names in vain (Ḥayei Adam 5:1; Mishna Berura 215:19). But in the framework of prayer or praise of God, it is a mitzva to mention them (see Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 12:1-2).

The Sages said that in a place where the Name is mentioned in a respectful manner, that is, by way of study and prayer, people merit wealth, as it is said (Shemot 20:20): "In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned I will come to you and bless you". But if it is mentioned in vain, it causes poverty (Nedarim 7b; Rosh and Nimukei Yosef there).

If a person mistakenly mentioned the Name of God, he should immediately continue and praise Him, for example by continuing and saying: "Blessed is He for ever and ever" or "Great is He and highly praised", and in this way he will correct his mistake, and it turns out that he did not mention the Name of God in vain (Rambam, Laws of Oaths 12:11).

The Sages said that one who hears his fellow deliberately mention the Name of Heaven in vain must place him under a ban (nidui) between himself and himself, and immediately release him from the ban (Nedarim 7b; Rambam, Laws of Oaths 9:12; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 334:37-38). One under a ban must withdraw from the company of people and conduct himself like a mourner; but since people were unrestrained in the sin of mentioning the Name in vain, the Sages ruled that on the one hand the one who hears should not be indifferent to his sin, and should ban him in order to express his protest, and on the other hand he should immediately release the ban so as not to multiply people under a ban who do not keep the law of their ban. And if he is able to rebuke his fellow for his sin – he should rebuke him.

sections.title_en: 5. Whether One Pronounces the Name of God During Study
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of Torah study includes studying the Torah, Prophets and Writings, and in the course of this reading the holy Names mentioned in them, as is the custom of Israel. It is likewise a mitzva to turn to God in prayer and in the course of this to mention His Name.

One who studies the Gemara and other sacred books of the Oral Torah may also read the Names mentioned in them (Mishna Berura 215:14). However, in practice, out of extra caution, lest he stop in the middle of a sentence and it turn out that he mentioned the Name without the proper respect, many are accustomed not to mention the Names of God explicitly when studying the Oral Torah. And wherever 'Ado-nai' is written they say 'Hashem', and when they read Names containing the letter 'heh', they replace it with the letter 'kuf': 'Elokim' instead of 'Elohim', 'Elokeinu' instead of 'Eloheinu', 'Kah' instead of 'Yah'. Some poskim reinforced their custom (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 215:2), but most poskim hold that it is preferable to read the Gemara while mentioning the Names explicitly (She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:81; and see Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:56, and Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:13), and some even considered changing the Names to be forbidden (Mikveh Ha-Mayim part 1, Yoreh De'ah 3). However, when there is a concern that the learner will stop in the middle of a sentence, and it will turn out that he mentioned the Name without the proper respect, it is preferable that he change the Names, as many are accustomed.

Also when one wishes to praise God in the course of a derasha or a dvar Torah, or when singing zemirot at a meal, by the letter of the law it is permitted to mention the Name of God. However, in practice many are accustomed to change it and mention Him by the epithet 'Hashem' or 'the Holy One, blessed be He', lest one stop in the middle of a sentence, and lest, if they mention the Name of Heaven a great deal, it appear as disrespect towards the holy Names.

Blessings are also mentioned in the Talmud, and some say that they should be read while mentioning the Name of Heaven (She'ilat Ya'avetz 1:81). But many hold that one should not mention the Name when reading them, for if he mentions the Name – it will be considered as saying a blessing in vain. Therefore he should change it and say 'Hashem' instead of 'Ado-nai'. But when teaching a child, or a person who does not yet know how to recite a blessing, one should read the blessing before him while mentioning the Name, and he too must repeat and practise the blessing while mentioning the Name. And after he has learned how to recite the blessing, when he reads the text of the blessings in the Talmud he should say 'Hashem', and not mention the Name of Heaven explicitly (Mishna Berura 215:14, following the Magen Avraham; Eliya Rabba, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav and others).[3]

It is permitted to play a recording of prayers containing the Name of Heaven, because the prohibition is to say the Name of Heaven in vain, but if a machine sounds the Name of Heaven there is no prohibition, provided that it is played in a clean place and in a manner that adds to the honour of Heaven and does not detract from it (Igrot Moshe, Yoreh De'ah 1:173).

notes_en.en: See below, halakha 14, note 15, that over the generations people adopted the custom of writing 'Elokim' instead of 'Elohim', especially in letters and correspondence. And since they grew accustomed to writing so, they also adopted the custom of pronouncing the Names with a change. And so wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (Oraḥ Ḥayim 215:2), that even in study "he should not say the Name explicitly, but should say 'Hashem', and likewise he should say: 'Elokeinu'". However, Rav Moshe Malka wrote about this (Mikveh Ha-Mayim part 1, Yoreh De'ah 3): "New ones who came lately, yeshiva students and ordinary learned men, adopted the custom of pronouncing the special Names with a kuf: 'Kel' instead of 'El', and 'Elokim' instead of 'Elohim'". But in his view it is not proper to act so; and just as one should not call the Name of God by the epithet 'Adoshem', for there is disgrace to the Name in this, as many wrote (Yosef Ometz, Yuzpa 349; Taz 621:2; Eliya Rabba there 10), so one should not pronounce the Names of God with an epithet and say 'Elokim' or 'Kel'; rather, one should read them as they are written in Scripture (and so wrote Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:13). And only in the blessings brought in the Talmud, out of concern for a blessing in vain, according to many one should change and say 'Hashem Elokeinu Melekh Ha-olam' (Yeḥaveh Da'at there). And according to She'ilat Ya'avetz (1:81), even in the blessings mentioned in the Talmud one should pronounce the Explicit Name, and there is no concern of a blessing in vain in this, for it is not a blessing but study.

sections.title_en: 6. The Prohibition of Erasing the Name
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden by the Torah to erase one of the Names by which God is called, as it is said concerning the idols of idolatry (Devarim 12:3): "and you shall destroy their name out of that place", and further on it is said (there 4): "You shall not do so to the Lord your God", meaning that it is forbidden to destroy His Name. One who deliberately erases one of the Names that were written in holiness, even one letter of the Name, transgresses a Torah prohibition and is liable to lashes (Shevu'ot 35a; Rambam, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:1; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:9). One who cuts a letter out of the Name of God, or covers it with ink, also transgresses the prohibition of erasing. Since it is forbidden to destroy the Name of God, the Sages said that a Torah scroll, tefillin and mezuzot that are worn out require geniza (as explained below, halakha 16).4

The epithets with which God is praised, such as: 'Gracious', 'Merciful', 'Great', 'Mighty', 'Awesome', 'Faithful' and 'Strong' – are not considered holy Names, since they can be said with the same meaning of a person too. Therefore, when necessary it is permitted to erase them, like the law of sacred writings that contain no holy Names (Rambam, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:5; Ein Yitzḥak 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5. See below halakha 15, note 18). However, since they are epithets of God, one should not say them in the toilet (Peri Megadim 85, Eshel Avraham 3; Birkei Yosef 7; Mishna Berura 11). 'The Holy One, blessed be He', 'Master of the Universe' and 'Hashem' also have the law of epithets.

It is permitted to erase a recording or a file, or to switch off a screen, that contains the Name of Heaven, since there is no substance of writing there. However, it is preferable to do so in a manner that does not erase the Name alone (see Igrot Moshe, Yoreh De'ah 2:142; Yabi'a Omer part 4, Yoreh De'ah 20; Tzitz Eliezer 13:1).

Although the Torah forbade erasing the holy Names, in order to make peace between a man and his wife the Torah permitted erasing the Explicit Name. When a connection formed between a married woman and a strange man, and her husband warned her not to be secluded with him, and nevertheless she was secluded with him, and her husband suspects that she committed adultery and is therefore forbidden to him, and his wife denies it and says that she did not commit adultery – the husband must bring her to the Temple, and the kohen asks her whether she committed adultery. If she admitted that she committed adultery, her husband divorces her. If she said that she did not commit adultery, they write on parchment the passage of the sota, in which the Name of God is mentioned, and erase the passage into water, and the woman would drink the water. After she drank it she was permitted to her husband. If she had sinned – her punishment was to die of an agonising illness. And from the time that the illnesses written in the Torah began to come upon her, she was forbidden to her husband, for these illnesses are the proof that she committed adultery. And if she had not sinned – she can continue to live with her husband for many good years. In this way peace would once again dwell between them (Bamidbar 5:11-31; Rambam, Laws of Sota 3:8; 15-16; 21-22).

notes_en.en: Keset Ha-Sofer (11:4, and Lishkat Ha-Sofer 9) wrote that even erasing part of a letter in the Name of God is forbidden. According to the Rema of Fano 36, it is forbidden by the Torah, and according to the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Yoreh De'ah, second edition 169), rabbinically. And according to the Peri Megadim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 32, Eshel Avraham 47), as long as the form of the letter remains there is no prohibition. And so wrote Responsa Maharshag (part 1, Yoreh De'ah 28). Drawing a line through the Name of God is also forbidden (Knesset Ha-Gedola, Yoreh De'ah 276:11; Birkei Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 276:25). Letters attached to the Name of God before it, such as the 'bet' of 'be-Elohim' – are not holy and it is permitted to erase them; and those attached to the Name after it, such as the 'khaf' of 'Elohekha' – have become holy, and are forbidden to be erased (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:9; Shakh 13; Taz 6; Keset Ha-Sofer 11:7).

sections.body_en:
There are three levels in the writing of holy Names and in the prohibition of erasing them:

a) A holy Name that was written with the intention 'for the sake of the holiness of the Name': its holiness is from the Torah, and likewise the prohibition of erasing it is from the Torah, and it is with this intention that the Names must be written in Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot (see above 10:7, on the definition of the intention).

b) A Name that was written out of recognition and belief that it is a holy Name, but without the intention of sanctifying it: it has holiness, but it is not valid for the writing of STaM. The poskim disagreed whether the prohibition of erasing it is from the Torah or from the words of the Sages. A Name that was printed out of recognition and belief that it is a holy Name is also forbidden to be erased (see below halakha 9).5

c) A Name that was written not out of recognition and belief in its holiness: it has no holiness and it is permitted to erase it. For example: one who writes the Name of God by mistake, such as one who intended to write 'Yehuda' and the 'dalet' was left out, so that the Explicit Name is before him – since he did not intend to write it, it did not become holy and it is permitted to erase it (Massekhet Soferim 5:4). Likewise one who writes a Name in a secular meaning, such as one who wrote 'Moshe went el (to) Aharon' – there is no holiness in the word 'el', and it is permitted to erase it (below halakha 8). And so the Sages said (Gittin 45b): "A Torah scroll that a heretic (min) wrote – is to be burnt". That is, there is no holiness in the Names written in it, and therefore when it was written with a missionary aim of turning Israel away from their religion, it is a mitzva to burn it (see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 13:6, note 6). In any case we have learned that if the holy Names were written not out of recognition and belief in their holiness according to the tradition of Israel, they have no holiness.6

notes_en.en: In the past idolaters were accustomed to write the names of their idols on their vessels, thinking that they would have blessing from this, and there were Jews who learned from them and wrote holy Names on their vessels, and the Sages ruled (Shabbat 61b) that one must cut out the place on which the Name was written and put it in geniza (see below note 11). However, they disagreed about the severity of the prohibition: some say that although he did not intend to write the Name 'for the sake of the holiness of the Name', since he wrote it out of recognition and belief in its holiness, it is forbidden by the Torah to erase it (Tashbetz 1:2; Ḥavot Ya'ir 16; Peri Ḥadash, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:6; Minḥat Ḥinukh 437:8; Birkei Yosef 274:24; Keset Ha-Sofer 11:2). And some say that the Names written on the vessels were written for the sake of the holiness of the Name, and therefore it is forbidden by the Torah to erase them, but when one wrote a holy Name out of recognition and belief in its holiness without the intention of sanctifying it, the prohibition of erasing it is rabbinic (Maḥaneh Efrayim, Laws of Torah Scroll, page 54a; Seder Mishna, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:1; Ein Yitzḥak 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5; Melamed Le-Ho'il 2:88; Aḥiezer 2, Yoreh De'ah 48. And Rav Herzog, in Piskei U-Khetavim 4, Yoreh De'ah 107, wrote that this is the view of most poskim). And many wrote that it is forbidden to erase it, without explaining whether the prohibition is from the Torah or rabbinic (Benei Yona 276:9; Yehuda Ya'aleh, Yoreh De'ah 269; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 29; Rav Pe'alim 4, Yoreh De'ah 31, and others). In any case, according to the great majority of poskim it is agreed that it is forbidden to erase a holy Name that was written out of recognition and belief in its holiness (although some permitted erasing it as long as it was not written for the sake of the holiness of the Name, and they are: Leḥem Yehuda 2:40; Mayim Ḥayim of Rav Mashash, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:369).

A STaM scribe who by mistake wrote the Name of God in the wrong place, for the sake of holiness, is forbidden to erase it (see above 10:14, how one acts in practice). Some say that even if he intended to write 'Yehuda' and by mistake wrote the Name Y-H-V-H, it is forbidden to erase it (Or Zarua, Tefillin 556, and Keset Ha-Sofer 12:1 inclined to this). However, according to the great majority of Rishonim and Aḥaronim, since it was written by mistake it is permitted to erase it, for so it is explained in Massekhet Soferim (5:4). And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (Yoreh De'ah 276:12) and Benei Yona (276:9). Likewise, a scribe who wrote in the Torah "elohim aḥerim" (other gods), whose meaning is idols, and erred and intended the Name of God – it has no holiness, because the intention of the Torah is idols, and the holiness of the Name cannot be applied to it (Tashbetz 1:177; Rema, Yoreh De'ah 276:2).
Gittin (45b): "A Torah scroll that a heretic wrote – is to be burnt; that a gentile wrote – is to be put in geniza". The Rambam explained (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:8): "A Jewish heretic who wrote a Torah scroll – it is burnt together with the Names in it, because he does not believe in the holiness of the Name, and wrote it only thinking that it is like other things; and since that is his view – the Name did not become holy, and it is a mitzva to burn it so as not to leave a name to the heretics or to their deeds". A 'min' is one who holds a foreign belief that is dangerous to Israel (see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 5, note 13); thus when the Names are written not out of recognition and belief in their holiness according to the tradition of Israel, they have no holiness (Lishkat Ha-Sofer, investigation 11; Maharam Schick, Oraḥ Ḥayim 66; Derekh Ha-Melekh of Rappaport and Even Ha-Azel, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah there; Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:50). And even if he wrote it out of belief in idolatry in partnership (shittuf), since he does not believe in its holiness in the way of Israel – it has no holiness, for with regard to Israel, according to all views, idolatry in partnership is forbidden like full idolatry (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 5:7). However, if he wrote it out of recognition and belief in the holiness of the Name according to the tradition of Israel, even though he is not Jewish, the Name became holy. But since it is not valid for reading in the Torah, the Sages ruled that it should be put in geniza, and this is what they said: "A Torah scroll that a gentile wrote – is to be put in geniza" (see above 10, note 1, in the explanation of the sugya). Thus it is the intention that determines the status of the Names.

sections.title_en: 8. Writing the Letters of Names in Another Meaning
sections.body_en:
Included in the third level, which has no holiness, are also words that are identical in their letters to the holy Names, but not in their meaning. For each of the holy Names also has a secular meaning that is not holy, and if the letters of the Name were written in a secular meaning, they have no holiness. For example, one of the Names is 'E-l', and this word can also serve as a preposition, such as: "Moshe went el (to) Aharon", and in this case the word 'el' has no holiness, and it is permitted to erase it and it does not require geniza.

Likewise, one of the Names is 'Tzeva'o-t', and this word can be used in a secular meaning, such as: "The allied armies (tzeva'ot) deployed their soldiers", and in this meaning there is no holiness.

And likewise concerning the Name 'Shadd-ai': if we wish to write 'my field' (ha-sadeh sheli) in one word, we write sadi, and in this word there is no holiness. And likewise there is an important book called 'Sedei Ḥemed', meaning many fields, and in this meaning there is no holiness. And there is no need to be concerned about using this word when the context makes clear that the Name of God is not meant.

And likewise concerning the Name 'Ado-nai': one can write it in another meaning, such as: "He founded its base on sockets (adnei) of fine gold", and in this meaning there is no holiness.

Similarly, there is no holiness in names of people or places that begin or end with a Name of God, such as: Yisrael, Shemuel, Ariel, Eliraz, or: Yedidya, Tovya, Yehonatan, Morya, Hodya. And likewise Eliyahu. And although these names were called after the Name of God, since they became names of people, there is no holiness in their meaning, and it is permitted to write them in their usual way without a hyphen or an omission (Tashbetz 1:177). And the same is the law concerning the name of the settlement 'Beit El': since the meaning is the name of a place and not a calling upon the Name of God, it has no holiness, and therefore it is permitted to write, erase and say the name of the settlement Beit El without restriction.7

All the more so, when one writes Germania or Anglia – one should not make any change, for there was never any intention in the names of these countries to allude to the Name of God.

Even the Explicit Name, composed of the four letters 'Y-H-V-H', has a further meaning: if a person wishes to write a word meaning 'will constitute' in the future tense, he would end up writing the letters of the Explicit Name (yehaveh in defective spelling). And since the context proves that the meaning is a secular sense, by the letter of the law there is no prohibition against writing it and it has no holiness. But it is not proper to do so, because this is the Explicit Name, the most sanctified of all the Names, and even writing it in another meaning involves a slight desecration of the Name. And one who needs to use this word should write it in full spelling – 'yehavveh' with a doubled vav – and then the word will not look like the Explicit Name.

Names of angels are not holy and therefore do not require geniza (Tashbetz 1:177).

notes_en.en: From a baraita in Massekhet Soferim (5:12) it follows simply that there is no holiness in names in which a Name of God is included and which are written as one word in Scripture, such as Tzuriel or Tzurishaddai. However, the place 'Beit El' is written as two words (the view of the Tanna Kamma), until here. Some learn from this that the word 'El' in 'Beit El' in the Torah is holy and forbidden to be erased. So wrote the Birkei Yosef (Yoreh De'ah 276:27), Melekhet Ha-Kodesh (beginning of parashat Lekh Lekha), R. Shlomo Ha-Kohen of Vilna, and R. Yitzḥak Schmelkes (Kuntres Be'er Be-Sadi, letters 2:23). And so it is brought in 'Shemot Kodesh Ve-Ḥol' (parashat Vayetze). On the other hand, according to many there is no holiness in the 'El' of the name 'Beit El' in the Torah, because its meaning is not 'the house of God' but the name of a place that was called after 'the house of God'. And they proved this from the custom of the scribes not to sanctify the name 'Beit El' that appears in the Torah; that is, although 'Beit El' is written as two words, it has no holiness (although today scribes are accustomed to be stringent in this). And likewise Onkelos did not translate it 'Beit Elaha', as he usually translates the word 'El'. And so the majority of poskim ruled, that it is not holy; so wrote the Eliya Zuta (142:2), the Peri Megadim (Oraḥ Ḥayim, Eshel Avraham 143:9), Sha'arei Yeshu'a (Yoreh De'ah 2) in the name of Responsa Ba'al Ginat Veradim, Yehuda Ya'aleh (2:107), the Ḥatam Sofer (6, Likkutim 5; 2:270), and Rav Guttmacher (Aderet Eliyahu, Yoreh De'ah 97). And if they said so concerning the name 'Beit El' in the Torah itself, all the more so there is no holiness in the name of the settlement when it is not written in the Torah. And so it was written in the responsa of the Chief Rabbi (5748-5749, 11), that there is no holiness in saying and writing the name of the settlement 'Beit El', and so is the custom (unlike the words of Aseh Lekha Rav 9:21). And it seems that there is no holiness in the names of songs such as 'Yah Ekhsof' or 'Lekha Eli', and they do not require geniza, but from the outset it is good to write them with a separating line (as brought below 14).

sections.title_en: 9. The Intention of the Writing Determines
sections.body_en:
As we learned (halakha 7), a holy Name that was written not out of recognition and belief in its holiness has no holiness and it is permitted to erase it. Similarly, about four hundred years ago, in the kingdoms of Sweden and Denmark in Europe, coins were struck bearing the Explicit Name (the Name Havaya – 'Y-H-V-H'), and the question arose whether they had holiness. In practice the poskim ruled that they have no holiness, because they were struck on a coin intended for secular use, and it is therefore clear that they did not intend holiness to take effect on it, but wrote it as a remembrance only; therefore it is permitted to trade with it and even to melt it down (Ḥavot Ya'ir 16; Mishna Berura 334:52). That is, in order for the Name to be holy it is not enough that those who make it know that it is the Name of God; rather, they must write it out of recognition and belief that it itself will be holy, and that all who see it will be aroused, on seeing it, to fear God. And since the intention of the kingdom was only to mention the Name, and not to cause a person who takes the coin to be aroused to fear Him, it has no holiness.

A further reason was given: the holiness of the Name takes effect only when it is written with the intention of writing a holy Name, whereas the craftsman who actually cast the coins cast them like other secular coins, without intention and awareness that he was creating a holy Name, like 'the act of a monkey' (Noda Bi-Yehuda, Yoreh De'ah, second edition 180).8

Similarly, an academic who wrote holy Names in a book or an article as a researcher, without recognition and belief in their holiness – the Names he wrote have no holiness, and there is no need to put them in geniza. In addition, the printing of these Names was done without the printer having any awareness that there were holy Names in the secular book, and this is a further reason why they have no holiness.

However, if a God-fearing academic wrote the holy Name out of recognition and belief in its holiness, there is holiness in what he wrote for himself. But in the academic book in which his article was printed there is no holiness, since the one who brought it to print (the initiator of the book) intended to publish a secular book, and the printer too is not aware that he is printing holy Names (below 17). In any case, since the writer is God-fearing, he should try to change the Names, so that no doubt arises lest holiness took effect on them.

Similarly, if a holy Name was printed by mistake in secular newspapers of God-fearing people, there is no obligation to put it in geniza, since the newspaper is mainly for secular purposes, and those who bring it to print and those who print it do not imagine that they are printing holy Names. But the editors of the newspaper must take care not to print holy Names by mistake, because this involves disrespect to the Name.

A person who maliciously wrote a holy Name on a classroom board or on a wall – since he did not write it out of recognition and belief in its holiness but by way of provocation and contempt, it has no holiness, and it is right to remove it soon, like the law of 'a Torah scroll that a heretic wrote' (Gittin 45b; above halakha 7). However, if they wrote a holy Name on the wall of a synagogue in order to honour it, and a need arose to renovate the wall – it is forbidden to erase the Name, since it was written out of recognition and belief in its holiness. Therefore they should place a sheet of paper or plastic over it, and stick down its edges in such a way that if they remove it, the Name will remain whole as it was, and they should plaster and paint over the paper or plastic as needed (Teshuva Me-Ahava 3:395). Similarly, if a teacher or a student erred and wrote a holy Name on the classroom board out of recognition and belief in its holiness, it is forbidden to erase it.

notes_en.en: The Ḥavot Ya'ir (15) wrote that it is permitted to destroy coins bearing the Name Havaya, since they did not intend the Name to be sanctified. And likewise we have learned (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 12:11) that, to make the distinction, if they found an image of idolatry on a vessel with which it is degrading to worship the idol, such as on an eating utensil, presumably they did not intend to sanctify the vessel, and therefore it is not forbidden for benefit like the law of idolatry. However, if a gentile goldsmith stamped the Name of God on a signet ring, since he was aware that he was creating a holy Name in order to arouse people to fear Him, the Ḥavot Ya'ir wrote that it became holy and it is forbidden by the Torah to destroy it (he further wrote in siman 184, concerning marital relations opposite printed books, that one of the reasons to be lenient is that the Names become holy through the intention of the writer or the printer, and since the printer did not print the Names in the books out of recognition and belief according to the tradition of Israel, they did not become holy). In practice, the great majority of poskim ruled concerning the coins like the view of the Ḥavot Ya'ir, among them: the Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel (Oraḥ Ḥayim 334:24), the Birkei Yosef (Yoreh De'ah 276:28), the Peri Megadim (Mishbetzot Zahav 334:16), Ḥesed La-Alafim (Laws of Torah Scroll 7), the Mishna Berura (334:52), and Yabi'a Omer (4, Yoreh De'ah 21). (However, the Maḥaneh Efrayim, Laws of Torah Scroll 54a, forbade destroying these coins.) In addition, the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Yoreh De'ah, second edition 180) permitted these coins because the worker who stamped the Name did not think at all about the holy Name on the coin, and made it 'like the act of a monkey'. And the Tzitz Eliezer (14:1) added this reasoning. Similarly, our master Rav Kook wrote (Da'at Kohen 161), concerning making relief plates for printing, that since the maker of the plates is not aware of the holy Names, he is like one 'acting unawares' (mit'asek) and the plates have no holiness (and see Igrot Moshe, Yoreh De'ah 1:172).

sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Shabbat 10b) that one of the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He, is 'Shalom', for God is the source of peace and of the completion between all created beings. Following on from this, Israel are accustomed to say 'Shalom' when they meet one another, and in this way they express the position that the bonds of friendship in Israel are founded on the Name of God, as it is said (Vayikra 19:18): "And you shall love your neighbour as yourself, I am the Lord", and in this way they deepen the friendship. In addition, in the blessing of 'Shalom' we express the destiny of our people: to reveal the unifying Name of God within the life of this world, and in this way to make peace in the world and to create in it a process of completion (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 22:10).

However, when the Sages counted the Names that may not be erased, they did not mention the Name 'Shalom'. Therefore its status is an intermediate status. That is, the word 'shalom' is not an essential Name of God, but expresses a human state of love and mutual completion; however, since peace flows from God, there is a certain holiness in this word (Rosh, rule 3:15; Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 276:16). Therefore, on the one hand, it is permitted to erase the word 'shalom', and there is no need to put in geniza a letter in which 'shalom' is written. On the other hand, it is forbidden to treat it with disrespect, and therefore it is forbidden to say 'Shalom' to a friend in filthy places such as a lavatory (Shabbat 10b; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 84:1).

And there are those who are stringent and hold that 'Shalom' too is one of the Names that may not be erased, and according to their view one must put in geniza a letter in which 'shalom' is written. And there are those who are less stringent and hold that it is permitted to erase the Name 'Shalom', but one should not write it on a letter that will be thrown away disrespectfully. Those who are stringent according to these views are accustomed to write 'shalom' in a letter while omitting the last letter (shalo'). And all this is when one writes 'shalom' as a word of blessing; but when one writes 'shalom' as a description of a state, such as relating that peace was made between neighbours or countries, even according to the stringent views there is no holiness in it.

In practice, the halakha follows the lenient view that it is permitted to write the blessing 'shalom' in a letter, and there is no need to put such a letter in geniza. And one who wishes to be meticulous – may be stringent.

Some forbid calling a person whose name is 'Shalom' by his name in filthy places (Magen Avraham). And some permit it, since the intention is the name of a particular person and not the concept of peace (Taz). In practice, since this is a dispute about a rabbinic matter, the halakha follows the lenient view, and those who are meticulous refrain from it (Mishna Berura 84:6).9

notes_en.en:
Shabbat (10b): Rav Hamnuna said in the name of Ulla: "It is forbidden for a person to greet his fellow with 'shalom' in the bathhouse, because it is said (Shofetim 6:24): And he called it: The Lord is shalom", for "the Name itself is called Shalom". The Rambam did not mention this law, and many understood from this that he did not rule it as halakha (Baḥ, Oraḥ Ḥayim 84:1; Peri Ḥadash, Oraḥ Ḥayim 85:2; Birkei Yosef 9, and others). However, the great majority of the Rishonim ruled it as halakha, and they disagreed about its status. According to the Rosh (Responsa 3:15), although one should not say 'shalom' in the bathhouse, "we have not found anyone who forbids erasing 'shalom', and in all letters 'shalom' is written and they are thrown away and erased". And this is because "it is not an essential name, but is called so on account of the action", and it is like 'Ha-Gadol', 'Ha-Gibbor' and 'Ha-Nora', in which there is no prohibition of erasing. And so wrote the Ritva (Shabbat 10b) in the name of Tosafot, the Shakh (276:16), the Peri Ḥadash (Oraḥ Ḥayim 85:2), and Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (Oraḥ Ḥayim 85:3). And so people were accustomed, as the Birkei Yosef (Yoreh De'ah 276:41) and Keset Ha-Sofer (11:17) wrote. And so wrote Kol Ya'akov (276:100) and Yabi'a Omer (part 4, Yoreh De'ah 22). On the other hand, according to Tosafot (Sota 10a), the Name 'Shalom' is one of the Names that may not be erased. And so it is implied by the 'attributed to the Ran' (on Shabbat 10b). And some did not count it among the Names that may not be erased, but since it has holiness, in that it is forbidden to mention it in the bathhouse, they ruled not to write it in full in letters and the like, so as not to treat it lightly, but to write shalo' and the like. So wrote the Rashba (Responsa 7:418) in the name of Rabbeinu Yeḥiel, the Tashbetz Katan in the name of the Maharam of Rothenburg 420, the Maharil (Minhagim, Yamim Nora'im 3), the Radbaz (1:220), Erekh Leḥem (Yoreh De'ah 276:10), the Mishna Berura (84:6), and the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (276:27-28, who was stringent not to erase it if it was written in full, except for a great need). And the Rema (Yoreh De'ah 276:13) wrote: "Some take care even with the word 'shalom' not to complete its writing", which implies that he does not hold that this is the halakha, but that some take care with this and there is room for their stringency. The Radbaz (1:220) added that the words of the stringent views apply specifically when one writes 'shalom' as a word of blessing, like one who blesses his fellow with the Name; but when one writes 'shalom' in the sense of peace between people or countries, even they would agree that it is permitted to erase it and throw it away.
Calling a person named 'Shalom' in the bathhouse: some say that included in the prohibition of saying 'shalom' in the bathhouse, it is also forbidden to call there by his name a person whose name is 'Shalom' (Baḥ, Oraḥ Ḥayim 84:1; Peri Ḥadash, Oraḥ Ḥayim 84:1; Magen Avraham 2). On the other hand, some say that the prohibition is only when one intends to bless his fellow with 'shalom', which is like blessing his fellow with the Name of God, but calling by name a person whose name is 'Shalom' is permitted, for this is not the Name of God but the name of a person (Taz, Oraḥ Ḥayim 84:3; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 1; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, Yoreh De'ah 276:28). In practice, the halakha follows the lenient view, and those who are meticulous refrain from saying it (Birkei Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 85:9; Mishna Berura 84:6).
Some were stringent not to say 'shalom' to someone who is not wearing a kippa, lest he return the greeting and it turn out that he says the Name of God with his head uncovered (Sedei Ḥemed, ma'arekhet alef, 313; Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim part 4, 40:24). However, there is no need to be concerned about this, because he returns the greeting in a respectful manner in which there is no disrespect. And so wrote Yabi'a Omer (part 6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 15) and Halikhot Shlomo (Prayer 2, Devar Halakha 26).

sections.title_en: 11. The Names of God in Other Languages
sections.body_en:
The Torah prohibition of mentioning in vain or erasing one of the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He, applies to the holy Names in the Hebrew language, which is the holy tongue, in which the world was created, and in which the Holy One, blessed be He, determined how human beings would call Him. But there is no intrinsic holiness in the foreign names that the members of the various nations gave to the Holy One, blessed be He, such as God in English, Gott in German and Yiddish, Allah (الله) in Arabic, or Bog (Бог) in Russian.

However, since the meaning of these names is sanctified, one should avoid saying them needlessly, and avoid saying them in a filthy place.

As for foreign names written in Hebrew letters or in foreign letters: according to most poskim, when necessary it is permitted to erase them, and there is no need to put them in geniza. But it is forbidden to put the pages on which they were printed to a degrading use, such as cleaning dirt; rather, they should be placed in the bin in a manner that involves no disrespect.

And some are stringent to put foreign names in geniza and to avoid erasing them without great need. Therefore they ruled to avoid writing them in newspapers or in a letter. The remedy for this is to change their writing by a separating line within the word (Go-d, or the same in Hebrew letters), or by omitting a letter (G-d, or the same in Hebrew letters).10

notes_en.en:
The Rambam wrote (Laws of the Sanhedrin 26:3) "that the names by which the gentiles call the Holy One, blessed be He – they are like all the epithets". And when necessary it is permitted to erase them like other sacred writings that contain no Names (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:5; above halakha 6). And so wrote the Radbaz (3:419), the Shakh (Yoreh De'ah 179:11), Keset Ha-Sofer (11:2) and the Mishna Berura (85:10). And so it is implied by all the poskim who did not mention a prohibition of erasing beyond the holy Names counted in the Shulḥan Arukh. However, even according to their view, one should not treat them disrespectfully (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, Yoreh De'ah 276:24). But it seems that placing them in a bin that is not especially filthy, or in a wrapping or bag inside a filthy bin – is not considered disrespect, since according to most poskim even a letter in which 'shalom' is written may be placed in the bin.
On the other hand, some forbade erasing them without great need. So wrote the Tashbetz (1:2), Panim Me'irot (1:45), Melekhet Shamayim (9:12), Kol Ya'akov (276:48), and others. And the Ḥavot Ya'ir (109) held like the stringent views when the foreign name is in Hebrew letters, and like the lenient views when it is in foreign letters. And in the Urim Ve-Tumim (27, Urim 2) he wrote not to write Names in letters even in a foreign language, and his words were brought in the Netivot Ha-Mishpat (27:2) and Aderet Eliyahu (Yoreh De'ah 97). In practice, out of concern for the stringent view, many are accustomed to write them with a separating line, such as 'Go-tt' (Aḥiezer 3:32).
Many hold that the law of saying a Name in a foreign language is like the law of erasing it (Rambam, Laws of the Sanhedrin 26:3; Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 179:11; Rabbi Akiva Eiger, first edition 25; Aḥiezer 3:32). And some inclined to be more stringent about saying it, because saying it disrespectfully looks more like an affront to the honour of Heaven. So wrote the Nimukei Yosef (Nedarim 1b) in the name of the Ritva, that there is no prohibition of mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain in a foreign language, but one who does so is rebuked. And so wrote the Radbaz (3:421), that although there is no prohibition, "it is good to take care with this too". And some are more stringent, not to say the Names of God in a foreign language outside the context of prayer or words of Torah. So wrote Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 14:8), the Responsa of the Geonim (Sha'arei Teshuva, siman 142), Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (Oraḥ Ḥayim 85:3), Ḥayei Adam (5:1), the Ḥatam Sofer (Nedarim 2a), Binyan Tziyon 68, the Mishna Berura (215:19) and the Kaf Ha-Ḥayim (215:27). And although here too the dispute is about a rabbinic matter, for the Names of God in a foreign language have the law of epithets, since saying Names in a foreign language in a disrespectful manner involves an affront to the honour of Heaven, more poskim inclined to stringency, and even the lenient ones wrote that it is good to take care with this; therefore above, concerning saying, I wrote according to the stringent view, whereas concerning erasing I brought first the view of the lenient ones as the main view.
Erasing a Hebrew holy Name written in foreign letters: according to most poskim it is rabbinically forbidden to erase a Name of God in the holy tongue when it is written in foreign letters, such as El, and therefore it must be put in geniza. So wrote Orḥot Ḥayim (Laws of the Love and Fear of God 6) in the name of R. Mordekhai in the name of the sages of Lunel, Bedek Ha-Bayit (Yoreh De'ah 276:10), Panim Me'irot (1:45), Pitḥei Teshuva (Yoreh De'ah 276:11), Minḥat Ḥinukh 437, Keset Ha-Sofer (11:2), Mikdash Me'at (276:110), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (276:24), and others. However, according to the Ḥavot Ya'ir (109), whatever is written in foreign letters – has no holiness at all. And it seems that even according to the stringent views, there is no need to put in geniza a newspaper in which the Name of God was written in foreign letters; it is only forbidden to erase it or treat it with disrespect. For above in halakha 9 it is explained that even a newspaper containing Names in Hebrew does not require geniza.

sections.title_en: 12. Care Not to Cause the Destruction of Names
sections.body_en:
In the Talmud (Rosh Ha-Shana 18b) it is related that the Greek kingdom decreed against Israel that they should not mention the Name of Heaven. When the Ḥashmona'im grew strong and defeated them, they saw a need to strengthen faith by mentioning the Name of Heaven, and instituted writing it in all documents. And so they would write: "In such-and-such year of Yoḥanan, High Priest to God (El) Most High". But this practice caused a mishap, for after a person paid his debt, many times he would throw the document away without putting the Name in geniza, and the Name of Heaven would be found lying in the rubbish. Therefore the Sages abolished this custom, and even established the day on which the custom was abolished as a festive day.

Similarly, as part of the duty of protecting the honour of the holy Names, one should not write holy Names on vessels. If one transgressed and wrote a holy Name on a vessel, it is forbidden to use it for secular purposes, and so that people will not err and use it, the Sages ruled to cut out the place on which the Name is written and put it in geniza, and afterwards the vessel will be permitted for use (Shabbat 61b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 276:13; Benei Yona).11

Similarly, one who has a holy Name written on his body, since it is forbidden to erase it, is forbidden to wash or anoint that place, lest he thereby bring about the erasure of the Name. However, if he needs to immerse in an immersion of mitzva, he should cover it with a covering that does not form a barrier and immerse. And although the water causes its erasure, since he needs to immerse for the sake of a mitzva, and the erasure is done indirectly (gerama) – it is permitted (Shabbat 120b).12

By Torah law there is no prohibition against writing the Name of God in a respectful way (Ḥavot Ya'ir 16), but the poskim wrote that one should not write holy Names outside sacred books, lest they come afterwards to disrespect (Rema, Yoreh De'ah 276:13). Therefore one must take care not to write holy Names in newspapers or in letters, nor in benchers, which sometimes come to disrespect. Likewise, one must avoid writing them in pictures hung in the synagogue, when there is a concern that they will wear out and be treated with disrespect (Sha'arei Teshuva, Oraḥ Ḥayim 11:3). However, when there is no concern that they will be treated with disrespect, it is permitted to write the Names or engrave them, such as on the Holy Ark or in front of the ḥazan (Mishna Berura 1:4).

One who photographs a place where there is a holy Name, such as a Holy Ark or a ḥazan's lectern, must take care not to print the picture with the holy Name, lest people not take care with its honour. Press photographers, whose photographs are distributed in thousands of copies, must especially take care with this. However, after the fact, if they erred and printed it, it does not require geniza (above halakha 9).13

notes_en.en: A baraita (Shabbat 61b; Arakhin 6a): "If (the Name of God) was written on the handles of vessels or on the legs of a bed – he should cut it out and put it in geniza". And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:6) and the Shulḥan Arukh (Yoreh De'ah 276:13). From this Responsa Ḥavot Ya'ir 16 learned that as long as he has not cut the Name of God off the vessel, the vessel is forbidden for use like things forbidden for benefit. And so wrote Benei Yona (276:13) and Mikdash Me'at (276:106). And according to Panim Me'irot (2:133), the vessel is not forbidden for benefit, and he may cover the Name in a respectful manner and use it in a respectful use, such as for drinking.

Indirect erasure of the Name: a baraita (Shabbat 120b): "If he had a Name written on his flesh – he should not wash, nor anoint, nor stand in a filthy place. If an immersion of mitzva came his way – he wraps reed-grass around it (so as not to be naked before the Name) and goes down and immerses". They explained in the Gemara (there) that although the immersion causes the erasure of the Name, there is no prohibition in it. For it is said (Devarim 12:4): "You shall not do so to the Lord your God", and they expounded: "doing is forbidden, causing indirectly – is permitted". According to many the permission is limited: according to the Rashba (there, s.v. 'Le-olam'), the permission is only in a situation where there is no certainty that the immersion will erase the Name. According to the Tashbetz (1:2), the permission is only in a situation where the Name is in any case about to be erased, as with a Name on one's flesh. According to the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Oraḥ Ḥayim, second edition 17) and the Ḥazon Ish (Yoreh De'ah 164:2), the permission is for the sake of a mitzva, such as an immersion of mitzva, and Har Tzvi, Yoreh De'ah 231 inclined to this. (And according to Tuv Ta'am Va-Da'at, first edition 239, the halakha does not follow the Gemara in Shabbat mentioned above, but the Gemara in Sukka 53a, from which it is implied that causing erasure is forbidden.) On the other hand, some hold that it is permitted to erase a holy Name indirectly even not for the sake of a mitzva. So wrote the Avnei Nezer (Yoreh De'ah 370:9), and the Beit Efrayim (Yoreh De'ah 61) inclined to this, and in practice permitted erasing indirectly by means of a child. And in the Aḥiezer (2:48) he permitted, where there is need, erasing indirectly by means of a non-Jew. However, even according to their view this permission is only when the Name is written not as part of a sacred book, but sacred writings are rabbinically forbidden to be erased even indirectly, as explained below 15.

The Tashbetz (3:301) wrote that one should not write holy Names at the opening of the ketubba, since the Sages made a festive day when they abolished the mention of the Name of God in documents. And so wrote the Rema (Yoreh De'ah 276:13): "And it is forbidden to write a Name from the outset not in a book, for it can come to disrespect, and therefore people take care not to write a Name in a letter". And so wrote the Levush (276:13), Yosef Ometz, Keset Ha-Sofer (11:17), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (276:27), and others. And in the Urim Ve-Tumim (27, Urim 2) he wrote not to write Names in letters even in a foreign language, like the stringent view in the previous section. And so people are accustomed from the outset, to write them with a change.
The 'Shiviti' plaque: about three hundred years ago many began to set up in synagogues 'Shiviti' plaques, on which they wrote the verse: "I have set (shiviti) the Lord before me always" (Tehillim 16:8). Some wrote this verse on parchment, sometimes beside Psalm 67, and placed it in the siddur, in order to arouse concentration. And some opposed this sharply, lest they cause disrespect to the holy Name (Sur Me-Ra Va-Aseh Tov 4:3, and the glosses of the Maharitza there; Divrei Yatziv, Yoreh De'ah 185). And some opposed a 'Shiviti' written on parchment, but not those fixed in the wall of the synagogue, for which there is no concern that they will come to disrespect (Sha'arei Teshuva 1:3, and in the name of his grandfather the Tevu'ot Shor; Rav Ḥarlap; Kol Ya'akov 276:92; Ḥelkat Ya'akov, Yoreh De'ah 156). And according to the Maharsham (1:96), writing the Name alone on the stand in front of the ḥazan is a disgrace, but as part of a verse it is permitted.
Various safeguards: Lishkat Ha-Sofer (11:28) wrote that one should avoid writing on the cloth that covers the Shabbat ḥallot holy Names that may not be erased, or the text of Kiddush, both because of disrespect to the Names and out of concern for the prohibition of erasing. And in the Igrot Moshe (Yoreh De'ah 2:134-135) he wrote that one should not print benchers with holy Names, because they commonly come to disrespect, and likewise one should not write a holy Name in wedding invitations. And so wrote the Tzitz Eliezer (14:1) concerning printing the Ten Commandments that are distributed in synagogues. And Benei Yona (276:13) wrote that "even in prayer books they adopted the custom of writing instead of the Name two yods or a heh and the like, and instead of Elohim to write alef and lamed joined". And so wrote the Sedei Ḥemed (ma'arekhet ha-mem, rule 12:9), that it is good to write the holy Names in the siddur with a change. According to the Ḥatam Sofer (part 6, Likkutim 5), it is permitted to write verses with holy Names on the parokhet, and he added that it is also permitted to write them on a gravestone, and holy Names were even written on the gravestone of the Rif. In the Igrot Moshe (Yoreh De'ah 2:136) he forbade writing a holy Name on jewellery, and the Tzitz Eliezer (16:30) inclined to this.
Writing Torah articles in newspapers: at the beginning of the printing of newspapers, some ruled not to write words of Torah in them, and one of the central reasons was that after reading the newspapers people were accustomed to use them for degrading things (Higayon Lev Ivri 2:10; Sedei Ḥemed 8, Pe'at Ha-Sadeh 12; Zaken Aharon 2:70). However, in practice, as newspapers became more widespread, the rabbis ruled that it is right to publish words of Torah in them without holy Names, in order to strengthen those near and far, and this is the prevalent custom of countless rabbis. In addition, today people are less accustomed to use newspaper pages for degrading things such as wrapping fish and cleaning dirt. In addition, many are accustomed to place newspapers in recycling bins, and there they are not treated with disrespect. Below in halakha 19 it will be explained that there is no need to put these articles in geniza.

sections.title_en: 13. Care with Names in Sacred Books and Newspapers
sections.body_en:
In the past people were accustomed to write in sacred books all the holy Names as they appear in Scripture, except for the Explicit Name. However, following the invention of printing sacred books multiplied, and the sages of the later generations saw that sometimes the books are not kept in their proper holiness, and pages of them are torn or burnt, and the Names in them are treated with disrespect. Therefore, in the last few centuries, various proposals began to be raised for writing the Names of God in a manner such that holiness would not take effect on them. Some were accustomed to write the Name with quotation marks inside it, such as E-lohi"m or Shadda"i. And some avoided this, lest readers mistakenly think that it is an abbreviation. A further solution was to replace the letter 'heh' in the holy Names with another letter. In the lands of Ashkenaz they wrote 'Elokim' instead of 'Elohim', and in the lands of Sepharad – 'Elodim'. Later they even used the letter 'kuf' to change the Name 'El' to 'Kel', and the Name 'Shaddai' to 'Shakai', and 'Tzeva'ot' to 'Tzevakot'. Following the writing of the Names in this way, people also grew accustomed to pronounce them so (above halakha 5).

On the other hand, some opposed changing the Names in sacred books: since these are sacred books, it is fitting that the Names be written in them as they are in the Torah, and only regarding the Explicit Name did they agree that it should not be written outside the framework of writing STaM. They further argued that writing the Name with a change of quotation marks or replacing letters with 'kuf' degrades the honour of the Name (as explained in the next halakha).

But when there is a great concern that the Names will be treated with disrespect and thrown away, such as in weekly Torah-portion leaflets, newspapers, workbooks and source sheets, it is agreed that the Names should be changed. This is so that their law will be like words of Torah without holy Names, and therefore there will be no concern of a Torah prohibition in destroying them. But since they want the learners to be able to understand the matter, the writers sought that the change should not make understanding difficult or cause confusion. Therefore, for example, they stopped using quotation marks such as E"l or Elohi"m, lest people think it is an abbreviation.

The most widespread form is to write a heh with an apostrophe (H') or a double yod (YY) or 'the Holy One, blessed be He' instead of one of the holy Names.14

notes_en.en:
Erasing the sign of a double yod: a baraita (Shevu'ot 35b): "If he wrote… 'Ad' of Ado-nai, 'Tzav' of Tzeva'ot – it may be erased", because it has no holy meaning. And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:4). However, Rabbeinu Ḥananel read: "If he wrote 'Ad' of Ado-nai… – they may not be erased". And Tosafot explained (Shevu'ot 35a, s.v. 'Be-Fer"ḥ') that according to his view, since he intended to write letters of the special Name, one must be more stringent and it is forbidden to erase them. In the Terumat Ha-Deshen (Pesakim U-Khetavim 171) he inclined to be stringent not to erase a double yod written as an abbreviation of the Name Havaya without great need, since the 'yod' is the beginning of the most sanctified Name. And the Aḥaronim were concerned for his view (Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 276:14; Shiyarei Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 276:16, and others).
Erasing the sign heh or dalet: in Benei Yona (276:20) he added that the letter 'heh' too, as expressing the Name Havaya, should not be erased without great need. And Melekhet Shamayim (9, Bina 28), Pitḥei Teshuva (276:16) and the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (24; 28) agreed with him. The basis of their words is the explanation of Tosafot of the view of Rabbeinu Ḥananel, as brought in the previous paragraph. And in Responsa Maharatz Ḥayot (1:11) he wrote that if he writes 'dalet' instead, it may be erased, for it is not a letter of the holy Name. And so our master Rav Kook did in his writings. However, in practice, people are accustomed to erase the sign 'heh', and so wrote Afarkasta De-Anya (1:60) and the Tzitz Eliezer (22:51), since according to the Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:4) and the Shulḥan Arukh (Yoreh De'ah 276:10) even with a 'yod' alone there is no prohibition, and all the more so with a 'heh'. And all this concerns erasing the sign, but it seems that there is no need to be concerned to put in geniza a letter in which the sign 'heh' is written, and all the more so printed matter with the sign 'heh'; rather, it is permitted to throw it in the bin.
Erasing B"H, Be-Ezrat Hashem, Im Yirtzeh Hashem and the like: simply, even according to the stringent views it is permitted to erase them, for this is an abbreviation of 'Barukh Hashem' and not 'Barukh Y-H-V-H' (Maharsham 1:159; Melamed Le-Ho'il, Oraḥ Ḥayim 113:20; Sho'el U-Nish'al 4, Yoreh De'ah 41; Yaskil Avdi 7, Yoreh De'ah 20; Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:78), and likewise in the other examples. And some wrote that without great need one should not erase B"H, and it is implied that according to their view it is preferable to write BS"D (Tzafnat Pa'ane'aḥ 196; Mayim Ḥayim of Rav Mashash, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:39). In practice, one may write B"H from the outset, and when necessary one may erase it.

sections.title_en: 14. Summary of the Proposals for Writing Holy Names
sections.body_en:
The proposal to write a heh with an apostrophe (H') or a double yod (YY) or 'the Holy One, blessed be He' suits a situation where one wishes to allude to the Name of God in general, and not specifically to one of His Names. The question is what the advice is when one wishes to write specifically 'Elohim' or 'El' or 'Shaddai' or 'Tzeva'ot'.

As mentioned in the previous halakha, a widespread form for writing each of the holy Names without its having holiness is to replace the letter 'heh' or another letter with the letter 'kuf'. So one writes: 'Elokim'; 'Kel'; 'Shakai' or 'Tzevakot'. However, many are not satisfied with this form, both because in their view changing the letters to 'kuf' is a jarring change that blemishes the honour of the Name, and because such a change slightly hinders the flow of reading and understanding.15

A nicer proposal is to insert a line in the middle of the Name, and thereby cause it not to become holy, such as 'E-lohim'. This proposal is cleaner in that it does not change the Name. And although some hold that this line does not help, since it is not considered a separating line but a joining one, the main view follows the lenient ones.16

A further proposal concerning 'Elohim' is to add a 'vav' and write 'Elohim' with a vav, as it is pronounced, and thereby it will have no holiness, since its writing in the Torah is without a 'vav'. The advantage of this proposal is that it does not change the Name and does not impair understanding, but it helps only with the Name 'Elohim'.17

notes_en.en: Writing 'Elokim' with a 'kuf': until about a hundred and fifty years ago, people were accustomed to write the Names without change in editions of the Gemara, the novellae of the Rishonim and the responsa. The Mabit even called his book 'Beit Elohim'. And so they were accustomed in Yemen (Olat Yitzḥak part 2, Oraḥ Ḥayim 74). However, in the lands of Ashkenaz, following the multiplication of the printing of sacred books, they began to write the Names with a change, such as joining the letters of the word 'El' into a single ligature. Also in old printings of the Talmud they sometimes wrote 'Elokim' or 'Elodim' instead of 'Elohim'. But the main care about this was in letters and correspondence, which are liable to come to disrespect. However, the Names 'Tzeva'ot' or 'Shaddai', which are less common, they did not change in books. And only in the last generation have some begun to change them too, perhaps because of the multitude of temporary writings that are treated with disrespect.

Separating the letters of the Name by a line: the Avnei Nezer (Yoreh De'ah 365) wrote that printers of sacred books who separate the letters 'yod' 'heh' with a line between them do not succeed in cancelling the prohibition of erasing the Name, because the letters remain as they were, and the line between them is considered in the eyes of the reader as joining the word into one. And so wrote Responsa Piskei Teshuva (1:134) and Minḥat Yitzḥak (9:62:3). However, in practice, since the line is intended to separate between the letters in order to cancel the holiness of the Name from them, and in addition, this form of writing is invalid for a Torah scroll, there is no prohibition of erasing the Name in them, especially when it is printing (Shraga Ha-Me'ir part 6, 156:2; Imrei Ya'akov part 2, 92; Ginzei Ha-Kodesh 7:14, note 29, in the name of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv; Halikhot Shlomo, Prayer 22:10, note 34). A further important reason to be lenient is that the one who brought it to print and the printer did not intend that there be holiness in this word, and therefore it has no holiness (see above halakha 9). And only with the Explicit Name, because of its great holiness, is it right to be stringent like the Avnei Nezer and not to make do with separating the letters by a line.

Writing 'Elohim' with a 'vav': in Responsa Zikhron Yosef (Steinhardt, Yoreh De'ah 17) he wrote that if a STaM scribe wrote 'Adonai' by mistake with a 'vav', this Name has no holiness, since the holy Name is not written so. And so wrote Lishkat Ha-Sofer (12:4) and the Ḥatam Sofer (in his glosses on Keset Ha-Sofer 12:8). Similarly, one who writes 'Elohim' with a 'vav' – it has no holiness, and one who erases it does not transgress the prohibition of erasing the Name. And seemingly one could argue that one who writes 'Elohim' with a vav creates a holy Name at the beginning of his writing, for at first he writes 'El', and after writing the 'vav' and the 'heh' – 'Eloah', and we have learned that when one writes 'El' of 'Elohim' it became holy and it is forbidden to erase it (Shevu'ot 35b). However, there the sanctification was because he intended to write a holy Name, but if from the beginning he intended to write 'Elohim' with a 'vav', then he did not intend to write a holy Name. And likewise we learned above (halakha 7) that when a Name was written in its form by mistake, it has no holiness. All the more so this is the law when the writer changed its form by adding a 'vav' with the intention that holiness should not take effect on it. This proposal also helps for writing the Name 'Ado-nai' with the addition of a 'vav' – 'Adonai' with a vav – except that in this way one may mistakenly think that the meaning is 'adoni', that is, a person who is my master.

sections.body_en:
As we learned (above halakha 1), the whole Torah is the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He, for it reveals His will to Israel. Therefore even in verses that contain no holy Names, there is holiness akin to the holiness of the Name. Therefore there is holiness also in the Scroll of Ester, even though it contains no holy Name. And from the time that they permitted writing the Oral Torah, this holiness extends also to books of the Oral Torah that contain no holy Names. Therefore books of Mishna and Gemara, Rishonim and Aḥaronim are also 'sacred books', and it is a mitzva to honour them and forbidden to treat them with disrespect. The words of the Sages (Avot 4:6) apply to them too: "Whoever honours the Torah – his person is honoured by people, and whoever profanes the Torah – his person is profaned by people". As Rabbeinu Yona explained (there): "that he should not put books on the ground, nor sit on a bench or a chair level with them". And so wrote the Shela (Massekhet Shevu'ot, Ner Mitzva 95): "Included in the honour of the Torah – to honour the books and the pages of books that have been damaged" (further on the honour of printed sacred books see above 9:9-10).

The law of books of the Oral Torah is like the law of verses of the Torah that contain no holy Names: it is permitted to erase them for the sake of correction or beautification, but it is forbidden to erase or destroy them needlessly. If one destroyed them in a degrading way – he transgressed the Torah prohibition of desecrating the Name, and if he destroyed them not in a degrading way – he transgressed a rabbinic prohibition.18

The poskim also treated books of Mishna and Gemara as books that contain no Names, even though from time to time the Names of God appear in them (Avnei Nezer, Yoreh De'ah 376:4; Har Tzvi 231; Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:39; Aseh Lekha Rav 3:28). Apparently, this is because the Names in them are few, and are not an essential part of the book as in a siddur or Tanakh, and the one who brings it to print and the printer do not have them in mind.

notes_en.en:
In the Gemara, Shabbat (115a), it is explained that in the period when it was forbidden to write translations, it was permitted to cause the erasure of a translation of the book of Iyov, since it was written in a forbidden manner and therefore had no holiness. And after it was permitted to write the Oral Torah, including translating the Tanakh, the Rishonim wrote that it is forbidden to erase words of the Oral Torah even indirectly, and it follows that they must be put in geniza (Tosafot there, s.v. 'Aliba'; Rosh 16:1; Mordekhai, Shabbat 396; Tur and Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 334:12). But for the sake of correction or beautification and the like it is permitted to erase in sacred books, for there is no affront to their honour in this. So wrote the Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:5), the Ḥinukh 437, the Tashbetz (1:2), Ein Yitzḥak (1:5), and many others.
The Rishonim explained that the prohibition of erasing sacred writings that contain no Names is rabbinic, for only concerning the erasure of holy Names is there a Torah prohibition.
