And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 6:8), the Ḥinukh 437, the Tashbetz (1:2), the Kesef Mishneh (Laws of the Foundations of the Torah there), Ein Yitzḥak (1:5), Zaken Aharon (2:70) and Har Tzvi (Yoreh De'ah 231). However, it seems that all that they said concerns the punishment of one who destroys sacred books, who is punished with lashes by rabbinic law, since there is no explicit Torah prohibition against destroying sacred writings that contain no holy Names; but care for their honour is included in the mitzva to sanctify the Name of Heaven and not to desecrate it (Vayikra 22:32; Rambam, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah 5:1). And likewise it is included in the mitzvot of the love and fear of God (Devarim 6:5; 6:13; Rambam there 2:1). (So wrote the Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34:17; and this can also be learned from the words of the Magen Avraham 154:9. See Ein Yitzḥak and Zaken Aharon mentioned above.)

sections.body_en:
There are two kinds of geniza: a) the geniza of STaM writings that contain holy Names; b) the geniza of sacred books written in ink on parchment but containing no holy Names, and likewise printed sacred books that contain holy Names.19

The first kind: the geniza of STaM writings that contain holy Names written for the sake of the holiness of the Name, including: a Torah scroll, the passages of tefillin and mezuzot, and likewise books of the Ḥumash, Prophets and Writings written in STaM script on parchment. The Sages said (Megilla 26b): "A Torah scroll that is worn out – is put in geniza beside a Torah scholar, even one who only studies halakhot". They further said that they must be put in geniza in an earthenware vessel, in order to preserve them as far as possible (Ran on the Rif), similar to the words of God to Yirmeyahu (Yirmeyahu 32:14): "and put them in an earthenware vessel, that they may last many days" (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 282:10; Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:5; Mishna Berura 22). Today people are accustomed to bury them in sealed plastic containers, for in this way they are preserved better than in earthenware jars (Ginzei Ha-Kodesh 15:2).

Likewise, in recent generations people have not been accustomed to bury them near the grave of a Torah scholar, but at the sides of the cemetery (Peri Megadim, Biur Halakha 154:5). Perhaps because they hold that if a place of their own can be found for them – it is preferable; and perhaps because they were afraid that wicked people would come to search for the sacred writings near the graves of the sages in order to treat them with disrespect, and therefore they buried them in a place where they could not find them (see Rashbash 62; Pitḥei Teshuva, Yoreh De'ah 282:13).

The second kind: sacred writings that contain no holy Names written 'for the sake of the holiness of the Name'. Included in this is a Scroll of Ester written 'for its sake' in STaM script, but which contains no holy Names. And likewise the law of printed Ḥumashim and siddurim, which do contain Names but are printed without an explicit intention for the holiness of the Name. And likewise Mishna and Talmud, Rishonim and Aḥaronim, the Names in which are printed without intention for the holiness of the Name. The geniza of these books is done by wrapping them in a sack and burying them in the ground at a depth of at least a handbreadth, in order to delay their destruction (Zera Emet 2:133). And some required burying them at a depth of at least three handbreadths (Knesset Yeḥezkel 17; glosses of the Ḥatam Sofer). When the geniza is buried at a great depth, or under the foundations of a building or a road, there is no need to wrap them, since burying them deep in the earth preserves them better than wrapping them in sacks at a depth of three handbreadths. And this is the prevalent custom today: not to wrap the geniza in sacks, but to bury it at building sites, in large and deep excavations in which many genizot can be buried in a manner that they will not be uncovered and treated with disrespect. There is no need to mark the place of the geniza, and above the place of the geniza one may build roads and houses without restriction.

notes_en.en: Some say that all sacred books require geniza in earthenware jars like a Torah scroll (Be'er Sheva 43; Eliya Rabba 154:7; Knesset Yeḥezkel 37; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, Yoreh De'ah 282:16; Zaken Aharon 1:9). On the other hand, in Responsa Zera Emet (2:133) he wrote as explained above, and wrote that this is the custom. And so the Peri Megadim testified (154, Eshel Avraham 9). And so wrote Zekhor Le-Avraham of Alkalai (part 3, Yoreh De'ah 60), Ikarei Ha-Dat (Oraḥ Ḥayim 8:12), the Kaf Ha-Ḥayim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:37) and the Ḥazon Ish (Yoreh De'ah 164). And so is the custom.

sections.title_en: 17. The Geniza of Printed Sacred Books
sections.body_en:
Following the invention of printing nearly six hundred years ago, the cost of printing books kept falling, and more rabbis printed their books, and more Jews bought them. About two hundred years after the invention of printing the question arose of how to act with the many books after they had worn out. For the room set aside for the geniza of books had filled up completely, and pages would spill over into the rubbish disrespectfully. And setting aside more space for geniza was difficult, because the areas that the gentile rulers allotted to the Jews and to the Jewish cemetery were very limited. And sometimes they buried the books in fields far from the town, and since the price of paper was high, gentiles came and dug in the ground and took them in order to use them for wiping in the lavatory. Therefore there were some of the great sages of Israel who ruled to burn the old books discreetly, so that they would not come to disrespect. But most poskim forbade burning old sacred books, and ruled that it is obligatory to put them in geniza by burial.

And some argued that if the printer was not aware that he was printing a sacred book, since he printed the book without belief and recognition that it is a holy book, it has no holiness and does not require geniza. However, in practice the poskim ruled that since the purpose of printing the book by the one who brought it to print was to print a sacred book, even if the printer was not aware of this, the book has holiness, and even if it contains no holy Names, after it is worn out it must be put in ordinary geniza.20

notes_en.en:
Responsa Shevut Ya'akov (part 3, 10:12) was lenient to burn discreetly printed sacred books that had worn out, and afterwards to bury their ashes. This was in order to prevent great disrespect to them, as brought above. However, according to most poskim there is no permission to burn them in order to save them from a concern of disrespect. So wrote Responsa Be'er Sheva 43, Knesset Yeḥezkel 37, the Magen Avraham (154:9), Sho'el U-Meshiv (third edition 1:15) and the Mishna Berura (154:24).
Above, 10:9, note 6, we learned that some even say that a valid Torah scroll can be written by printing, when the printer intends 'for the sake of the holiness of a Torah scroll' and 'for the sake of the holiness of the Name'. And so wrote the Mas'at Binyamin, the Taz, Divrei Ḥamudot, the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, and others. On the other hand, some invalidate it, and so wrote the Maharashdam, the Baḥ, the Ḥavot Ya'ir, Benei Yona, and others. And so it was ruled as halakha. However, it seems that all agree that there is holiness in printed sacred books, that it is forbidden to destroy them and they require geniza. And so wrote the Maharashdam (Yoreh De'ah 184), that it is forbidden to use pages of worn-out printed sacred books as material for book bindings, because in this way he destroys them with his own hands.
However, as brought above in halakha 9 and note 8, according to the reasoning of the Noda Bi-Yehuda (Yoreh De'ah, second edition 180), if the gentile printer did not intend to print a holy book, it has no holiness. And the Ḥavot Ya'ir 184 added this reasoning concerning the law of marital relations opposite printed books. However, it seems that even according to this reasoning there is rabbinic holiness in printed books (above note 18), and they only argued that the Names that were printed have no additional holiness. In addition, one must also take into account the aim of the one who brings it to the printing house, who wants to print a sacred book, and since the printer acts as his agent, the printed book has holiness (see Maḥaneh Efrayim, Agents and Partners 11). And so wrote the Melamed Le-Ho'il (2:89), that the intention of the one who brings it to print has significance. And so it is implied by the Ya'avetz (Migdal Oz, Even Boḥan 2:30), who required putting in geniza a sacred book that was printed by a gentile. And this is the inclination of the poskim: to treat printed books as books that have holiness, and only as an addition to a main reason for leniency did they also add the reasoning that the printer did not intend holiness. And likewise we find that they forbade marital relations even opposite printed books: R. Yosef Molkho (Responsa Ohel Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2), the Ḥokhmat Adam (Beit Ha-Nashim 128:10) and the Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh (150:6). And likewise they forbade using printed sacred books for secular purposes or for a degrading use: Teshuva Me-Ahava (1:9), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (Yoreh De'ah 271:39), the Tzitz Eliezer (21:42), and Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu (Responsa Ma'amar Mordekhai 1:14). However, many added the reasoning that the holiness of printed books is lesser, in order to rely on the majority of poskim who hold that one covering suffices at the time of marital relations (Davar Moshe part 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5; Ohel Yitzḥak, Oraḥ Ḥayim 6). And so wrote Yabi'a Omer (part 4, Yoreh De'ah 21) concerning entering the toilet with one covering. See Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 2:17, note 17.
Some argue that the words of the Aḥaronim about the holiness of printed books concerned printing most of whose operation was by hand, but today printing is automatic, and therefore there is no holiness in printed sacred books in our day (see Yeḥaveh Da'at 6:57; Halakha Berura 40:8:6). However, it seems that it makes no difference how the machine works: as long as a person operates the machine – there is holiness in the books he prints. And see above 2, note 11, on the law of making tzitzit threads by machine, and Peninei Halakha, Pesaḥ 12:4, concerning machine matza.
A new reasoning for leniency was written in the Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:39): since there is no mitzva to write words of the Oral Torah, there is no obligation to put sacred books such as Gemarot in geniza after they have been used, for all their holiness stems from their designation for study, and once they have finished studying from them – their holiness has lapsed, and it is permitted to place them respectfully in the bin. However, in practice, as we have learned above, the great majority of the poskim do not agree with his reasoning.

sections.title_en: 18. The Problem in Our Day, and the Recycling Proposal
sections.body_en:
Over time, in many places the status of the Jews improved, and it already became possible to find a place for respectful geniza in the ground. However, at the same time the number of books and printed pages rose immeasurably, and the trouble involved in collecting them for geniza became enormous. Especially in crowded places, where they had to transport the huge quantity of geniza to distant places where suitable tracts of land were found for burying it.

As a solution to the problem, some proposed placing sacred books in containers intended for paper recycling. For one who places sacred books in the recycling container does not perform an action involving disrespect or erasure, but only causes the books to be taken to the recycling plant. And in the recycling plant the pages requiring geniza mix with secular writings and are nullified in the majority, so that one can say that the workers are not destroying sacred books, but their intention is for the majority of pages, which are secular. But they permitted this for ordinary sacred books, and not for Ḥumashim and siddurim, in which there are many holy Names, and the ones who bring them to print and the printers are aware of the Names mentioned in them. But they were not concerned about the few Names in ordinary sacred books, since they did not intend to sanctify them (above halakha 9), and generally also without awareness of their existence (above 15). They further argued that in the process of geniza too the books are often treated with disrespect, so that placing them in recycling does not greatly affront their honour.

On the other hand, many hold that it is forbidden to place the books in recycling containers, since by doing so one causes their destruction, and the halakha requires putting them in geniza in a manner that delays their destruction. And so it is accepted to rule. The prevalent solution today is to charge money for the geniza, and since the geniza is done for payment, it is done in an orderly and respectful manner.21

notes_en.en: Some hold that it is permitted to place in recycling containers ordinary sacred books such as the Gemara and commentaries (in which there is no awareness that they contain Names, even though they truly do contain Names, as explained at the end of halakha 15). First, they relied on the view of the Shevut Ya'akov and the Igrot Moshe (note 20). And they also relied on the reasoning of the Noda Bi-Yehuda, according to which when the printer is not aware of the holiness of the things he prints, they have no holiness (above halakha 9, note 8). And although the great majority of the poskim did not accept their words, they held that in a pressing situation one may rely on the lenient views. Moreover, placing in recycling is lighter than the ruling of the Shevut Ya'akov to burn the books, or the ruling of the Igrot Moshe not to put them in geniza. For in placing them in recycling containers there is no disrespect at all, and there the pages on which the words of Torah appear mix with and are nullified in a many times greater quantity of secular matter. And so wrote Si'aḥ Naḥum 74, Rav Uri Dasberg (Teḥumin 3, p. 307 ff.) and Rav Shabtai Ha-Kohen Rappaport (Alon Shevut 28, pp. 68-77). However, it is accepted to rule that sacred books require geniza, and just as the view of the Shevut Ya'akov and the Igrot Moshe was rejected, so the proposal to recycle sacred books should be rejected. It should be added that today in the Land of Israel, which is being progressively built up, it is relatively easy to find places for geniza in the deep excavations made in preparation for building houses and roads.

sections.title_en: 19. Proof Sheets, Worksheets, Leaflets and Newspapers
sections.body_en:
Before printing a book, one sheet is printed for proofing, in order to see that the pages come out straight and in order. In the past this was also done in order to make final corrections. Some are stringent and hold that proof sheets require geniza. However, according to most poskim they do not require geniza, because they did not become holy. There are two reasons for this: first, they were intended for proofreading and not for study; second, they were printed with the understanding that they would be destroyed at the end of their use. And since this is the view of most poskim, and in addition the basis of the law is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient view, and one may place the proof sheets in the bin in a respectful manner, such as wrapped in paper or in a bag, or in recycling containers.

And it seems that this is the law of booklets of words of Torah that are attached to newspapers or sent by post, which their recipients do not intend to study from, and likewise Shabbat leaflets that remained in the synagogue without anyone studying from them at all. For since it is known to those who bring them to print that some of them will not be studied, as long as they have not been studied from, their law is like the law of proof sheets, which do not require geniza.

Likewise, tests, worksheets and exercise books, since their main purpose is to activate the students and not that they should study from them – did not become holy, and one may follow the lenient view concerning them and place them in recycling or in the bin wrapped in a bag. But notebooks of words of Torah that a person intends to keep in order to go back and study from them – require geniza.

Torah leaflets, weekly Torah-portion sheets and source sheets that were studied from: some say that since their purpose is temporary study only – they did not become holy, and it is permitted to place them in recycling containers (Yeḥaveh Da'at of Rav Ḥazan, part 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 10), or in the bin wrapped in a bag (Si'aḥ Naḥum 74). And although one who wishes to be lenient like them may do so, it is more correct to follow the view of most poskim, who hold that since they were intended for study and were studied from – they became holy, and must be put in geniza like other sacred writings.

Similar to this is the law of a leaflet whose main content is sacred matters: even though it also contains secular articles, since its main content is sacred and it was also studied from – it is preferable to put it in geniza. But since it was also intended for secular matters, the lenient view is strengthened.

But a leaflet whose main content is secular and which contains Torah articles may be placed in recycling containers or in the bin. All the more so there is no need to put in geniza the Torah articles printed in a newspaper most of which deals with news and other secular matters. And there is no need to check whether holy Names slipped into them, for even if they erred and printed a holy Name in them, the intention of the one who brought it to print and of the printer was to print secular matters, and therefore the article did not become holy (above note 8).

However, the writers of articles in newspapers, and likewise the editors of the newspapers, bear the responsibility to take care not to write holy Names (above, end of note 13). The editors of booklets of words of Torah and of source sheets too must try that there be no holy Names in them, for although people are stringent to put them in geniza, one should minimise creating a situation in which holy Names must be put in geniza; and only in sacred books that are destined to last many days does one write holy Names from the outset (above halakha 13).[22]

notes_en.en:
Proof sheets ('korektin'): the printing houses were accustomed to throw the proof sheets into the rubbish, and many times gentiles took them and treated them with great disrespect, such as for wrapping food and wiping in the lavatory. And the poskim disagreed about how one must act with them: Ikarei Ha-Dat (Oraḥ Ḥayim 8:12) forbade destroying them with one's own hands. And likewise the Aḥiezer (Yoreh De'ah 48) forbade destroying them except by means of a gentile and indirectly. And according to Magen Gibborim (Shiltei Ha-Gibborim 154:2) there is even a Torah prohibition in this. On the other hand, according to many there is no holiness in pages printed in order to correct the book from printing errors by means of them, because their designation is not for study but for proofreading, and therefore they did not become holy and it is permitted to destroy them by burning so that they will not be treated with further disrespect (Ein Yitzḥak, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5-7; Rav Elyashiv, Kovetz Teshuvot 2:6). And the Netziv (Meshiv Davar 2:80) reasoned that since they were printed for brief use, they did not become holy and it is permitted to destroy them. And some were lenient even with proof sheets of Ḥumashim and siddurim that contain many Names (Meshiv Davar there; Zaken Aharon 2:70; Yeḥaveh Da'at of Rav Ḥazan 3:10). And similarly the Mor U-Ketzi'a 154 wrote that it is permitted to use them for binding, but not to treat them with disrespect. And in Responsa Avnei Nezer (Yoreh De'ah 376) he was more lenient, that even books of the Oral Torah, as long as people have not begun to study from them, holiness has not yet taken effect on them, and there is no prohibition against destroying them.
And it seems that the main view follows the lenient ones, for even concerning a holy Name written out of belief and recognition the poskim disagreed whether the prohibition of erasing it is from the Torah, and the view of the majority of poskim is that the prohibition is rabbinic (above note 5). And even according to those who hold that the prohibition of erasing these Names is from the Torah, the Rishonim wrote that the prohibition of erasing books of the Oral Torah is rabbinic, as explained in halakha 15 and note 18. And although books of the Oral Torah contain a few Names, the Aḥaronim treated them as books that contain no Names, apparently because the one who brings them to print and the printer do not have them in mind (as explained at the end of halakha 15). And even if the Names in the proof sheets are many, such as in Ḥumashim and siddurim, since they were not intended for study, the printers do not have them in mind (and their intention is decisive, as explained above in halakha 9 and note 8). And so the Tzitz Eliezer (3:1) wrote in practice, that one may burn the proof sheets, but not throw them into the rubbish in a degrading way. As we will learn further on, according to several poskim placing them in the bin inside a box or a bag in the rubbish is not considered disrespect, for the bag or box preserves their honour.
Weekly Torah-portion leaflets, source sheets and the like are more stringent than proof sheets, and must be put in geniza. For proof sheets were not intended for study at all, whereas from weekly Torah-portion leaflets and source sheets people study (Zaken Aharon 2:70 inclined to this; and so wrote Minḥat Yitzḥak 1:18; Minḥat Asher, Talmud Torah 9; and so hold those who require geniza for words of Torah in a newspaper, brought below). However, some hold that since the study from them is one-time, they did not become holy, and there is no need to put them in geniza; rather, it is permitted to place them in recycling containers (Yeḥaveh Da'at of Rav Ḥazan, part 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 10), or in the bin wrapped in a bag (Teshuvot Ve-Hanhagot 1:553; Si'aḥ Naḥum 74). And although the whole discussion is rabbinic, it is accepted to rule that from the outset one should put in geniza source sheets and leaflets whose purpose is Torah study. And those who are lenient to place them in recycling or in the bin wrapped in a bag – have something to rely on, for as explained above, the dispute is about a rabbinic matter. And those who print source sheets and weekly Torah-portion leaflets bear the responsibility to take care that there are no Names in them, and if they did not take care they bear the sin, as brought above in halakha 12. But after the fact, since the intention was to print words of Torah without holy Names, their law is like words of Torah without holy Names.
With tests and worksheets in Torah subjects, the lenient view seems more correct, since their main designation is to test the student's knowledge or to activate him. And likewise concerning sukka decorations adorned with verses, since they were not intended for actual study.
Booklets of words of the Oral Torah that are distributed to the public, in the case where their recipients do not intend to study from them, and likewise weekly Torah-portion leaflets that remained in the synagogue without anyone studying from them at all, it seems do not require geniza. For since it is known to those who bring them to print and to the printers that some of them will not be studied, they did not become holy through their printing. But if people studied from them, their law is as explained above.
Words of Torah printed in newspapers and leaflets: some are stringent and hold that one should cut out the words of Torah and put them in geniza (Rav Grunfeld in Yerushat Peleta 29; Yaskil Avdi 7, Yoreh De'ah 20; Halikhot Shlomo, Prayer 20, note 72; R. Shlomo Min Ha-Har in Teḥumin 3, in response to the article of Rav Dasberg; Ḥevel Naḥalato 10:38). And some ruled so from the outset, and after the fact permitted recycling them (Rav Elyashiv in Kovetz Teshuvot 2:6; Aseh Lekha Rav 3:28; Be-Mar'eh Ha-Bazak 5:89). However, some hold that one goes according to the main content of the newspaper or leaflet: if its main content is secular – it was printed with that in mind, and there is no need to put the words of Torah in it in geniza (Minḥat Yitzḥak 1:18. And similarly in the Shevet Ha-Levi 5:162). And they may be added to the lenient views even regarding weekly Torah-portion leaflets and source sheets, as explained above. And they should be placed in recycling containers or in the bin in a manner that the secular pages cover the page with the words of Torah. All the more so this is the law concerning Torah articles in secular newspapers, for although on one side words of Torah are printed, on the other side there may be things entirely opposed, and putting them in geniza involves disrespect. (In Ginzei Ha-Kodesh 12:1; 3, he was stringent to put in geniza street notices containing a halakhic instruction to dress modestly, or food packaging bearing a halakhic instruction about which blessing to recite. But there is no need to be concerned about this, since they did not print them with the intention of printing sacred matters.)
